rationale: A wins because it understands that the ugliest unanswered question is the story, not a PR inconvenience: "Klarna's AI did the work of 700 agents. It won't say how many people lost their jobs." B has useful material, but it trips over its own feet by asserting "Klarna's AI is now handling disputes" when the update only says advocates worry about AI handling disputes. A also keeps the five tempting angles from becoming mush by refusing duplicates and requiring the first-question proof before anyone pitches.
gaps_in_A: "When a Klarna customer disputes a charge, a chatbot may be the first one to rule on it" is carefully hedged, but still leans close to implying the assistant touches disputes before that fact is proven.
"Decay: week" appears on every viable angle; the judgment may be defensible, but it reads formulaic where the IPO angle likely has a filing-driven clock.
The contact-center benchmark angle could ask for customer satisfaction by segment or case type, not just "a satisfaction, repeat-contact, or reopen metric."
gaps_in_B: "Klarna's AI is now handling disputes" is an invented fact. The update says advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes, not that Klarna confirmed the assistant handles them.

"Klarna says its AI now handles two-thirds of support chats" and "Klarna won't say how many of the jobs it cut were actually replaced by AI" split one labor-accountability story into two padded versions.

"Klarna's profitability narrative leans on AI-driven cost reduction" overstates the update. Klarna is profitable and has filed to go public; the facts do not say the profitability narrative leans on AI.
"The most-mocked category of enterprise AI might actually be working" repeats a refused angle A correctly killed: speed and containment are not satisfaction, accuracy, or efficacy.
